chapters.title: Introduction to Mobile and Mobile Programming

questions.question: What is a mobile device? Explain different features of mobile device.
questions.answer:
A mobile device (handheld computer) is a computing device small enough to be held and operated in the hand, typically with an LCD/OLED touch screen and designed for portable, on-the-go use (smartphones, tablets, PDAs, e-readers, smartwatches).

Features:

  1. Portable — light and compact; can be carried and used anywhere.
  2. Personal — customisable with wallpapers/apps/settings; belongs to one user.
  3. Companion — always with the user; constant communication, entertainment and productivity support.
  4. Easy usage — intuitive touch interfaces; usable without technical training.
  5. Connected — internet connectivity and links with online services and smart devices.

questions.question: What do you mean by mobile device? List and explain any four popular programming languages used for developing mobile application.
questions.answer:
A mobile device is a general term for any handheld computer or smartphone — for example tablets, e-readers, smartphones, PDAs, portable music players, smartwatches and fitness trackers. Four popular mobile programming languages:

  1. Java — the original official Android language (now Kotlin is preferred); huge ecosystem and community; more verbose for beginners.
  2. Kotlin — Google's official Android language since 2019; interoperates with Java, removes boilerplate (no semicolons, fewer null-pointer issues), beginner friendly.
  3. C# — similar to Java, garbage-collected, cleaner syntax; used with Xamarin / .NET for cross-platform mobile apps.
  4. Swift — Apple's modern language for iOS/macOS; safe, fast, expressive; the standard choice for iPhone/iPad development (Objective-C is the legacy option).

questions.question: What is a smart mobile device? Explain different platforms used in mobile devices.
questions.answer:
A smart mobile device is a mobile device with computing capability: it runs an operating system, installs applications, connects to the internet and offers sensors, multimedia and communication features (smartphones, tablets, smartwatches).

Platforms:

  • Android (Google) — open-source, used by many OEMs; Java/Kotlin; huge device range and customisation.
  • iOS (Apple) — proprietary; Swift/Objective-C; known for smoothness, security and integration.
  • KaiOS — lightweight feature-phone platform with basic apps.
  • Windows Phone (discontinued) — Microsoft's former platform.
  • Tizen / HarmonyOS / Wear OS — niche devices (TVs, wearables) and emerging ecosystems.

questions.question: What are different mobile application development approaches? Explain in details.
questions.answer:
1. Native development — build separately per platform with the platform SDK and language (Kotlin/Java for Android; Swift/Objective-C for iOS). Best performance and full device-feature access; highest cost (two codebases).
  2. Cross-platform development — one codebase deployed to both platforms using frameworks such as React Native, Flutter or Xamarin. Saves time/cost by reusing code; may lag native performance and newest features.
  3. Web app development — HTML/CSS/JavaScript served in the mobile browser. Platform-independent and easy to update; limited performance and device access.
  4. Progressive Web Apps (PWA) — web apps with app-like capabilities (offline caching, installable icon, device APIs). Middle ground: no app store required, better reach, still browser-sandboxed.

questions.question: What is Android? Explain different categories of mobile devices.
questions.answer: Android is a mobile operating system developed by Google (debuted 2008 with Android 1.0) and an open-source software stack for phones, tablets, TVs and more. Categories of mobile devices: mobile phones (voice-centric), low-end devices (basic, limited features), mid-end devices (budget smartphones with a balance of price and performance), high-end devices/flagships (top specifications), and non-phone devices such as tablets, smartwatches, fitness trackers and portable media players.

questions.question: Explain Android architecture with a suitable diagram.
questions.answer:
Android is a stack of software components, commonly shown as five sections in four main layers:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ APPLICATIONS  (Calculator, Contacts, apps)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ APPLICATION FRAMEWORK                       │
│  Activity Manager · Window Manager ·        │
│  Content Providers · View System ·          │
│  Notification · Resource · Location Manager │
├──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┤
│ LIBRARIES            │ ANDROID RUNTIME      │
│  Surface Manager ·   │  Core libraries +    │
│  Media Framework ·   │  ART (was Dalvik VM) │
│  SQLite · OpenGL ES ·│                      │
│  WebKit · libc · SSL │                      │
├──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┤
│ LINUX KERNEL  (drivers, memory, security)   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  1. Linux kernel — memory/process management, device drivers, security; the core services all layers depend on.
  2. Libraries + Android Runtime — libraries (Surface Manager for display composition, Media Framework, SQLite, OpenGL ES, WebKit, libc, SSL…) and the runtime that executes each app in its own process. The runtime moved from Dalvik (JIT) to ART (AOT compilation) for better performance.
  3. Application framework — managers/APIs that developers build against: Activity Manager, Window Manager, Content Providers, View System, Notification Manager, Resource Manager, Telephony/Location Manager.
  4. Applications — user-facing apps (system + installed).

questions.question: What is surface manager library? How DVM is different from ART?
questions.answer:
Surface Manager is the Android library responsible for composing the display: it combines drawing surfaces from multiple applications into one screen image (handling windows, off-screen buffers and smoothing), so apps can share the screen without conflicts. It also manages 2-D/3-D graphics composition.

  • Dalvik VM (DVM): Used up to Android 4.4; ART: Default runtime from Android 5.0
  • Dalvik VM (DVM): Executes .dex bytecode with JIT compilation at runtime; ART: Compiles apps ahead-of-time (AOT) during installation
  • Dalvik VM (DVM): One VM instance per app, register-based; ART: Same per-app model, but precompiled native code
  • Dalvik VM (DVM): Slower app start and higher battery use for heavy apps; ART: Faster execution, better battery and memory behaviour

questions.question: Draw the hierarchical directory structure of an Android application. How can you use string and string array in Android? Explain.
questions.answer:
MyApp/
├── app/
│   ├── manifests/AndroidManifest.xml
│   ├── java/  (Kotlin/Java sources; package folders)
│   ├── res/
│   │   ├── drawable/      images
│   │   ├── layout/        activity_main.xml …
│   │   ├── menu/          options_menu.xml …
│   │   ├── mipmap/        launcher icons
│   │   └── values/        strings.xml, colors.xml, arrays.xml, themes.xml
│   └── build.gradle (module)
├── gradle/  ·  build.gradle (project)  ·  settings.gradle

Strings: define <string name="app_name">My App</string> in res/values/strings.xml; reference it as @string/app_name in layouts or getString(R.string.app_name) in code. String arrays: <string-array name="fruits"><item>Apple</item>…</string-array> in res/values/arrays.xml; used with android:entries="@array/fruits" (Spinner/ ListView) or getResources().getStringArray(R.array.fruits) in code.

questions.question: How to create AVD's? How to use spinner in android? Explain with suitable example.
questions.answer:
Creating an AVD: Android Studio → Tools → AVD Manager → Create Virtual Device → choose hardware profile (e.g., Pixel phone / tablet) → select a system image (API level; download if needed) → name the AVD and set RAM/storage → Finish → press ▶ to launch the emulator, then Run the app on it.

Spinner: a drop-down that lets the user pick one item; items come from a string array or adapter.

<Spinner android:id="@+id/spinner"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:entries="@array/fruits" android:prompt="Select an item"/>

spinner.setOnItemSelectedListener(new AdapterView.OnItemSelectedListener() {
    @Override public void onItemSelected(AdapterView<?> p, View v, int pos, long id) {
        Toast.makeText(getApplicationContext(), p.getItemAtPosition(pos).toString(),
                       Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show();
    }
    @Override public void onNothingSelected(AdapterView<?> p) { }
});

questions.question: List and explain any five widgets used in android programming.
questions.answer:
1. TextView — displays read-only text (android:text, android:textSize).
  2. EditText — accepts user input (android:hint, android:inputType such as text/number/password).
  3. Button — clickable trigger for actions (android:text); handled with setOnClickListener.
  4. ImageView — displays images/drawables (android:src, android:scaleType).
  5. CheckBox / RadioButton — two-state toggles (independent vs. exclusive within a group). (Also common: Spinner for one-of-many selection.)

questions.question: What is an event? How many ways to handle events in android programming?
questions.answer:
An event is an action or occurrence (click, long press, touch, key press, focus change) generated by the user or system and delivered through Android's FIFO event queue. Handling concepts:

  1. Event listener — interface with a single callback on a View (OnClickListener.onClick, OnLongClickListener, OnTouchListener, OnKeyListener, OnFocusChangeListener, OnMenuItemClickListener).
  2. Event registration — attaching the handler to the listener (view.setOnClickListener(...)).
  3. Event handler — the callback method that performs the action when the event fires.

Ways to handle: anonymous inner class listeners, activity implementing the listener interface, lambda expressions, declaring android:onClick in XML, and overriding framework methods (onTouchEvent, onKeyDown).

questions.question: What is the difference between android:layout_gravity and android:gravity attribute in linear layout. Create an android application that will convert distance entered into Kilometers into Meters using Table Layout.
questions.answer:
• android:gravity — sets the alignment of the content inside the view (text in a TextView, children in a LinearLayout).
  • android:layout_gravity — sets the alignment of the view itself within its parent container.
<TableLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:padding="16dp">
    <TableRow>
        <TextView android:text="Kilometers:" android:padding="4dp"/>
        <EditText android:id="@+id/kmEdit" android:inputType="numberDecimal"/>
    </TableRow>
    <TableRow>
        <Button android:id="@+id/convertButton" android:text="Convert"/>
    </TableRow>
    <TableRow>
        <TextView android:id="@+id/meterView"/>
    </TableRow>
</TableLayout>

Button convert = findViewById(R.id.convertButton);
convert.setOnClickListener(v -> {
    double km = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.kmEdit)).getText().toString());
    ((TextView) findViewById(R.id.meterView)).setText((km * 1000) + " meters");
});

questions.question: Differentiate RelativeLayout and ConstraintLayout with suitable example.
questions.answer:
• Aspect: Positioning; RelativeLayout: Relative to parent/other views; ConstraintLayout: Flexible constraints (to parent, siblings, guidelines)
  • Aspect: Complexity; RelativeLayout: Gets deeply nested for complex UIs; ConstraintLayout: Fewer nested levels; flat hierarchies
  • Aspect: Performance; RelativeLayout: Slower with deep nesting; ConstraintLayout: Generally good even for complex layouts
  • Aspect: Alignment; RelativeLayout: Fine-grained attributes (alignParent…, alignTop…); ConstraintLayout: Constraints + bias + guidelines + chains
  • Aspect: Flexibility; RelativeLayout: Less responsive across sizes; ConstraintLayout: Excellent responsiveness
  • Aspect: Best for; RelativeLayout: Fixed alignments/positions; ConstraintLayout: Responsive, complex UIs

Example (the same label centred over a button):

<!-- RelativeLayout -->
<RelativeLayout ...>
    <Button android:id="@+id/btn" android:layout_centerInParent="true"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="OK"/>
    <TextView android:layout_above="@id/btn" android:layout_centerHorizontal="true"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Label"/>
</RelativeLayout>

<!-- ConstraintLayout -->
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout ...>
    <Button android:id="@+id/btn" android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:text="OK"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintBottom_toBottomOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"/>
    <TextView android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Label"
        app:layout_constraintBottom_toTopOf="@id/btn"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="@id/btn"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="@id/btn"/>
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

questions.question: Develop an android application to calculate perimeter of rectangle using LinearLayout.
questions.answer:
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical" android:padding="16dp">
    <EditText android:id="@+id/lengthEdit" android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:hint="Length"
        android:inputType="numberDecimal"/>
    <EditText android:id="@+id/breadthEdit" android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:hint="Breadth"
        android:inputType="numberDecimal"/>
    <Button android:id="@+id/calcButton" android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:text="Calculate Perimeter"/>
    <TextView android:id="@+id/resultView" android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"/>
</LinearLayout>

public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity {
    @Override protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main);
        findViewById(R.id.calcButton).setOnClickListener(v -> {
            double l = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.lengthEdit)).getText().toString());
            double b = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.breadthEdit)).getText().toString());
            ((TextView) findViewById(R.id.resultView)).setText("Perimeter = " + 2 * (l + b));
        });
    }
}

questions.question: Explain AbsoluteLayout’s positioning attributes. Develop an Android calculator using AbsoluteLayout with two numeric inputs, separate multiplication and division buttons, and a TextView displaying the result.
questions.answer:
Important AbsoluteLayout attributes: android:layout_x and android:layout_y — the exact coordinates of a child within the parent (in dp). The layout is deprecated because fixed coordinates do not adapt to different screen sizes/densities.

<AbsoluteLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="match_parent">
    <EditText android:id="@+id/num1" android:layout_x="40dp" android:layout_y="40dp"
        android:layout_width="200dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:inputType="numberDecimal" android:hint="First number"/>
    <EditText android:id="@+id/num2" android:layout_x="40dp" android:layout_y="110dp"
        android:layout_width="200dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:inputType="numberDecimal" android:hint="Second number"/>
    <Button android:id="@+id/mulBtn" android:layout_x="40dp" android:layout_y="180dp"
        android:text="Multiply"/>
    <Button android:id="@+id/divBtn" android:layout_x="160dp" android:layout_y="180dp"
        android:text="Divide"/>
    <TextView android:id="@+id/resultView" android:layout_x="40dp" android:layout_y="250dp"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content" android:layout_height="wrap_content"/>
</AbsoluteLayout>

findViewById(R.id.mulBtn).setOnClickListener(v -> {
    double a = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.num1)).getText().toString());
    double b = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.num2)).getText().toString());
    ((TextView) findViewById(R.id.resultView)).setText("Result = " + (a * b));
});
findViewById(R.id.divBtn).setOnClickListener(v -> {
    double a = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.num1)).getText().toString());
    double b = Double.parseDouble(((EditText) findViewById(R.id.num2)).getText().toString());
    ((TextView) findViewById(R.id.resultView)).setText(b != 0 ? "Result = " + (a / b) : "Cannot divide by zero");
});

questions.question: Why fragment is needed in android? Write a java code only to send data from one activity to another activity using implicit intent.
questions.answer:
Why fragments: they make UIs modular and reusable, allow one activity to host different UI combinations (e.g., list + detail side by side on tablets, swapped on phones), support dynamic add/replace at runtime, and can be retained across configuration changes.

Implicit-intent Java code (no target class named):

Intent send = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND);
send.setType("text/plain");
send.putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, "Hello from my app");
send.putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_SUBJECT, "App message");
startActivity(Intent.createChooser(send, "Share via"));

questions.question: Explain different types of API. Develop an android application to pass name and age of customer from one activity to another. [4+6]
questions.answer:
API types:

  1. Web APIs (web services) — accessed over HTTP; used by many clients (phones/tablets/PCs); e.g., REST/JSON services.
  2. Local APIs — local middleware services on the machine; e.g., TAPI (Telephony API), .NET.
  3. Program APIs — make a remote program appear local via RPC; e.g., SOAP.

Pass name + age between activities:

// FirstActivity
EditText nameEdit = findViewById(R.id.nameEdit);
EditText ageEdit  = findViewById(R.id.ageEdit);
findViewById(R.id.nextButton).setOnClickListener(v -> {
    Intent i = new Intent(FirstActivity.this, SecondActivity.class);
    i.putExtra("name", nameEdit.getText().toString());
    i.putExtra("age", Integer.parseInt(ageEdit.getText().toString()));
    startActivity(i);
});

// SecondActivity.onCreate
String name = getIntent().getStringExtra("name");
int age = getIntent().getIntExtra("age", 0);
((TextView) findViewById(R.id.detailView)).setText("Name: " + name + "\nAge: " + age);

questions.question: Differentiate activities and fragments. Develop an Android app whose first fragment accepts a rectangular box’s length, width and height; a Volume button passes them to a second fragment, which calculates and displays the volume in a TextView.
questions.answer:
• Activity: Standalone screen component with its own lifecycle; Fragment: Modular UI part hosted inside an activity
  • Activity: Represents a whole screen; Fragment: Represents a portion of a screen
  • Activity: Communicates via intents; Fragment: Communicates via host activity / interfaces
  • Activity: Recreated on configuration change (unless handled); Fragment: Can be retained across configuration changes
  • Activity: Declared in the manifest; Fragment: Declared in layout or created by FragmentManager
// FirstFragment: inputs + button
public class FirstFragment extends Fragment {
    @Override public View onCreateView(LayoutInflater inf, ViewGroup c, Bundle b) {
        View v = inf.inflate(R.layout.fragment_first, c, false);
        v.findViewById(R.id.volumeButton).setOnClickListener(x -> {
            String l = ((EditText) v.findViewById(R.id.lengthEdit)).getText().toString();
            String w = ((EditText) v.findViewById(R.id.widthEdit)).getText().toString();
            String h = ((EditText) v.findViewById(R.id.heightEdit)).getText().toString();
            Bundle args = new Bundle();
            args.putString("l", l); args.putString("w", w); args.putString("h", h);
            SecondFragment second = new SecondFragment();
            second.setArguments(args);
            ((MainActivity) requireActivity()).showSecondFragment(second);
        });
        return v;
    }
}
// SecondFragment reads getArguments() and computes volume = l * w * h, then shows it.

questions.question: Develop an android application to input your Name, Age, gender and other personal information. Pass and display this information in another activity.
questions.answer:
<!-- activity_first.xml (extract) -->
<EditText android:id="@+id/nameEdit"  android:hint="Name"/>
<EditText android:id="@+id/ageEdit"   android:hint="Age" android:inputType="number"/>
<RadioGroup android:id="@+id/genderGroup">
    <RadioButton android:id="@+id/male"   android:text="Male"/>
    <RadioButton android:id="@+id/female" android:text="Female"/>
</RadioGroup>
<Button android:id="@+id/submitButton" android:text="Submit"/>

// FirstActivity
findViewById(R.id.submitButton).setOnClickListener(v -> {
    Intent i = new Intent(FirstActivity.this, SecondActivity.class);
    i.putExtra("name", ((EditText) findViewById(R.id.nameEdit)).getText().toString());
    i.putExtra("age", ((EditText) findViewById(R.id.ageEdit)).getText().toString());

// SecondActivity: read getStringExtra for name/age/gender and display in a TextView.

questions.question: How to handle different device orientations (portrait/landscape) in an Android application?
questions.answer: Options: (a) let the system recreate the activity and save/restore state with onSaveInstanceState() / onCreate(Bundle); (b) provide alternative resources in res/layout-land/ (and values-land/) so each orientation gets its own layout; (c) handle the change yourself with android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" and re-layout in onConfigurationChanged() (least preferred); (d) use retained fragments/ViewModels to keep data across recreation.

questions.question: What is menu? Develop an android application to create popup menu having menu item "Edit", "Copy", "Paste", "Redo" and "Undo".
questions.answer:
A menu presents common actions/options to the user; Android has three types — options menu (action bar), context menu (long-press), and popup menu (floating, anchored to a view).

<!-- res/menu/popup_menu.xml -->
<menu xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <item android:id="@+id/edit" android:title="Edit"/>
    <item android:id="@+id/copy" android:title="Copy"/>
    <item android:id="@+id/paste" android:title="Paste"/>
    <item android:id="@+id/redo" android:title="Redo"/>
    <item android:id="@+id/undo" android:title="Undo"/>
</menu>

Button anchor = findViewById(R.id.menuButton);
PopupMenu popup = new PopupMenu(this, anchor);
popup.getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu.popup_menu, popup.getMenu());
popup.setOnMenuItemClickListener(item -> {
    if (item.getItemId() == R.id.edit)  { /* handle */ }
    // … copy, paste, redo, undo
    return true;
});
popup.show();

questions.question: Explain the process of creating options menu in android app with suitable program.
questions.answer:
1. Define items in res/menu/menu_main.xml.
  2. Inflate the menu by overriding onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu) in the activity.
  3. Handle clicks by overriding onOptionsItemSelected(MenuItem).
  4. (Optional) Add app:showAsAction="ifRoom" for action-bar items.
<menu xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <item android:id="@+id/action_settings" android:title="Settings"/>
    <item android:id="@+id/action_about"    android:title="About"/>
</menu>

@Override public boolean onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu menu) {
    getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu.menu_main, menu);
    return true;
}
@Override public boolean onOptionsItemSelected(MenuItem item) {
    switch (item.getItemId()) {
        case R.id.action_settings: /* … */ return true;
        case R.id.action_about:    /* … */ return true;
        default: return super.onOptionsItemSelected(item);
    }
}

questions.question: What is Toast? Develop an android application to create alert dialog to input any number and then calculate factorial of number and display the result in Toast.
questions.answer:
Toast is a small transient message shown for a short time without interrupting the user or requiring any action.

EditText numberEdit = new EditText(this);
numberEdit.setInputType(InputType.TYPE_CLASS_NUMBER);

AlertDialog.Builder builder = new AlertDialog.Builder(this);
builder.setTitle("Factorial")
    .setView(numberEdit)
    .setPositiveButton("Calculate", (dialog, which) -> {
        int n = Integer.parseInt(numberEdit.getText().toString());
        long fact = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) fact *= i;
        Toast.makeText(this, "Factorial = " + fact, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show();
    })
    .setNegativeButton("Cancel", null)
    .show();

questions.question: What does android APK file contain? Develop an android application with context menu having menu item "Red", "Yellow", "Green", "Black" and "Blue" etc. and change background color of layout when user selects a menu item accordingly.
questions.answer:
APK contents: compiled .dex code, resources (layouts/drawables/strings), the AndroidManifest.xml, native libraries (if any), assets, META-INF signing certificates/keys, and the resources.arsc index — effectively the packaged, signed application.

// MainActivity
View layout = findViewById(R.id.mainLayout);
registerForContextMenu(layout);

@Override public void onCreateContextMenu(ContextMenu menu, View v, ContextMenu.ContextMenuInfo info) {
    super.onCreateContextMenu(menu, v, info);
    menu.add("Red"); menu.add("Yellow"); menu.add("Green"); menu.add("Black"); menu.add("Blue");
}
@Override public boolean onContextItemSelected(MenuItem item) {
    switch (item.getTitle().toString()) {
        case "Red":    layout.setBackgroundColor(Color.RED);    return true;
        case "Yellow": layout.setBackgroundColor(Color.YELLOW); return true;
        case "Green":  layout.setBackgroundColor(Color.GREEN);  return true;
        case "Black":  layout.setBackgroundColor(Color.BLACK);  return true;
        case "Blue":   layout.setBackgroundColor(Color.BLUE);   return true;
        default: return super.onContextItemSelected(item);
    }
}

questions.question: What are uses of fragments? How fragments are differing from activity?
questions.answer:
Uses: modular/reusable UI units; adapt layouts to screen size (phone vs tablet); combine multiple fragments in one activity; dynamic UI changes (add/replace/remove at runtime); retain state across configuration changes; divide complex screens into manageable parts.

Differences: see the Activity vs Fragment table in Q18 (lifecycle, UI ownership, communication mechanism, configuration-change behaviour, hosting).

questions.question: How do you find view element in your program? Which dialog boxes can you use in your android application?
questions.answer:
Finding views: findViewById(R.id.viewId) (returns the view; cast in Java for typed widgets); with View Binding / Data Binding, references are generated automatically.

questions.question: Provided that a MYSQL database named "Bank" with table named Customer with columns (account_no, name, account_type and amount) — connect remotely and display customers whose deposit amount is greater than 5000.
questions.answer:
Server side: a small PHP endpoint queries MySQL and returns JSON:

<?php
$conn = new mysqli("localhost", "root", "", "Bank");
$result = $conn->query("SELECT * FROM Customer WHERE amount > 5000");
$json = array();
while ($row = $result->fetch_array()) {
    $json["data"][] = array("account_no" => $row["account_no"], "name" => $row["name"],
        "account_type" => $row["account_type"], "amount" => $row["amount"]);
}
echo json_encode($json);
$conn->close();
?>

Android side (network on a background thread; parse JSON; show in a ListView):

// In a background thread (AsyncTask/Thread) — INTERNET permission required
URL url = new URL("https://yourhost/bank.php");
HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();
BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(conn.getInputStream()));
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); String line;
while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) sb.append(line);
reader.close();

JSONObject root = new JSONObject(sb.toString());
JSONArray data = root.getJSONArray("data");
String[] rows = new String[data.length()];
for (int i = 0; i < data.length(); i++) {
    JSONObject c = data.getJSONObject(i);
    rows[i] = c.getString("account_no") + " - " + c.getString("name")
            + " (" + c.getString("account_type") + ") : " + c.getDouble("amount");
}
runOnUiThread(() -> ((ListView) findViewById(R.id.bankList))
        .setAdapter(new ArrayAdapter<>(this, android.R.layout.simple_list_item_1, rows)));

implementation 'com.google.android.gms:play-services-maps:18.2.0'

public class MapsActivity extends AppCompatActivity implements OnMapReadyCallback {

questions.question: Provided that a SQLite database named "BookStore" with a table named Book (book_id as Integer, name as Text, author as Text) — insert three book records and display the book information.

public class DBHelper extends SQLiteOpenHelper {
    public DBHelper(Context c) { super(c, "BookStore", null, 1); }
    @Override public void onCreate(SQLiteDatabase db) {
        db.execSQL("CREATE TABLE Book (book_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, author TEXT)");
    }
    @Override public void onUpgrade(SQLiteDatabase db, int o, int n) { }
}

// Insert three records
SQLiteDatabase db = new DBHelper(this).getWritableDatabase();
ContentValues cv = new ContentValues();
cv.put("book_id", 1); cv.put("name", "Android Basics");      cv.put("author", "A. Author");   db.insert("Book", null, cv);
cv.clear();
cv.put("book_id", 2); cv.put("name", "Kotlin in Action");    cv.put("author", "D. Jemerov");  db.insert("Book", null, cv);
cv.clear();
cv.put("book_id", 3); cv.put("name", "Head First Java");     cv.put("author", "K. Sierra");   db.insert("Book", null, cv);

// Display
Cursor c = db.rawQuery("SELECT * FROM Book", null);
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
while (c.moveToNext()) {
    sb.append(c.getInt(0)).append(" · ").append(c.getString(1))
      .append(" · ").append(c.getString(2)).append("\n");
}
((TextView) findViewById(R.id.bookView)).setText(sb.toString());
c.close(); db.close();

func factorial(_ n: Int) -> Int {

    if n > 1 { for i in 2...n { result *= i } }
    return result
}
print(factorial(5))   // 120

questions.question: What do you mean by mobile programming? Explain life cycle of mobile application development.
questions.answer: Mobile programming is the set of processes and procedures for writing software for small, wireless computing devices (PDAs, enterprise digital assistants, phones). Life cycle: two interlinked components — the front-end (app on the device) and back-end services (support it) — developed through an iterative/agile cycle: Develop → Test → Release → Deploy → Monitor → Analyze, then repeat with improvements. Back-end decisions include build-vs-buy for services and self-hosted vs third-party hosting.

questions.question: Differentiate RelativeLayout and LinearLayout with example.
questions.answer:
• LinearLayout: Arranges children linearly (horizontal/vertical); RelativeLayout: Arranges children relative to parent/each other
  • LinearLayout: layout_weight distributes space/size; RelativeLayout: Uses layout_toRightOf, layout_below, layout_alignParentTop, …
  • LinearLayout: Good for simple linear forms (sign-up screens); RelativeLayout: Good for complex arrangements (store layouts)
  • LinearLayout: Can be nested inside RelativeLayout; RelativeLayout: Can be a child of LinearLayout
